extraction.body: Help Net Security newsletters : Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – subscribe here! An attacker has been offering “desktop apps” for three large US payroll and HR platforms that have never released one, Allure Security have found. Anyone who runs the installer gets a copy of ScreenConnect , a legitimate remote access tool, configured to let the attacker control the computer without the user knowing. According to Ryan Merritt , Director of Security Research at Allure Security, all three providers deliver their products as web applications accessed through a browser, with mobile companion apps, and none offers a desktop application for its current platform. The researchers did not disclose which providers were impersonated. Three payroll desktop-app lures (Source:Allure Security) The people most likely to install such an app are those who run payroll. Merritt says unattended access to their machine is “a path to diverting or draining an entire company’s payroll.” The lure pages were created with Lovable, an AI app builder that turns a text prompt into a web page. The operator did not remove the build metadata, and the tags left in the pages show the workflow. The attacker built each page in Lovable, saved its preview as a single HTML file with a browser extension called SavePage WE, and hosted the file on Vercel. The metadata shows the snapshot was taken from the operator’s own Lovable preview. Each page carried the brand’s logo, product screenshots, a live-chat widget and a download button. The pages were hosted behind Vercel’s bot-challenge screen. “Automated scanners hit the challenge page and stopped, without accessing the lure, which is why the pages left almost no public scanning footprint while they were live,” added Merritt. The download button linked to a release file in a GitHub repository. One GitHub account held a separate repository for each brand, and each published the same file under a brand-specific name. The file is an installer of about 64 MB built with NSIS, the Nullsoft Scriptable Install System. When it runs, it first opens the genuine, Microsoft-signed .NET Desktop Runtime 8.0.26 installer, with a progress window that ends on a success message. It then runs msiexec with the /qn flag, which installs ScreenConnect in the background with no interface. A standard Windows elevation prompt appears between the two steps. “So the only thing the victim sees is a real Microsoft installer finishing normally. The promised payroll app never opens, because it does not exist, and the one window that did appear belonged to Microsoft. Nothing on screen looks like malware,”Merritt wrote. The ScreenConnect client is configured for unattended access, with the “under control” banner, tray icon and connection notifications disabled. The client installs as a Windows service, runs in Safe Mode, creates scheduled tasks and loads on the Windows sign-in screen, allowing access before a user logs in. The server and a working payload were in use in August, a month before the branded pages appeared. Those installers were signed with a certificate issued to “Dennis Miller” by SSL.com, which revoked the certificate on July 24, 2026, its issue date. September samples were unsigned. The GitHub files were downloaded 291 times, a figure that includes researchers and sandboxes. At the time of analysis, 32 of 70 security engines flagged the installer as malicious. “On reach, the numbers are modest, but when you consider the potential impact of drained company payroll accounts, they are non-trivial,” noted Merritt. How victims reached the pages, whether through ads, search results or email, has not been established. Microsoft reported in March 2026 on a campaign that impersonated workplace apps such as Teams, Zoom and Adobe Reader to deploy ScreenConnect and other remote access tools. Huntress reported in September 2026 on rogue ScreenConnect clients spread through tech support lures. The researchers also found fake desktop apps for cryptocurrency exchange, wallet and DeFi brands using the same tooling and the same type of ScreenConnect payload. They attribute these to a separate operator cluster, with a different signer, certificate authority, code-hosting accounts and live-chat licenses. The three fake payroll pages, the command-and-control domain and the GitHub profile hosting the installers have since been taken down by Allure Security. “If your company runs a cloud payroll or HR platform, the most useful thing you can do this week is check whether yours actually ships one, and tell employees that a download the vendor does not offer is not an upgrade. It is the attack,” concluded Merritt.

The server and a working payload were in use in August, a month before the branded pages appeared. Those installers were signed with a certificate issued to “Dennis Miller” by SSL.com, which revoked the certificate on July 24, 2026, its issue date. September samples were unsigned. It is the attack,” concluded Merritt.

sources.title: Meta’s Muse Charm looks like a Tamagotchi, but it’s tapping into a much newer trend
passages: Is Meta’s just-announced Muse Charm a playful device that will make AI more approachable to everyday consumers, or will it be yet another flop in a long list of AI hardware gadgets that didn’t take off, like the Ai Pin, Rabbit, or Friend pendant?
If that’s the privacy tradeoff in gaining access to free AI — Meta said it will monetize Muse by taking a small fee from transactions — consumers could be willing to take the risk.

To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations.
In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement.
It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses.
However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference.
It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch.

Often meant as a way to repurpose an older device , the concept of the Apple Watch keychain or charm has been growing in popularity, fueled by TikTok videos showing different ways to use the watch when not on your wrist.
One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030 .
Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post- Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags.

Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case , had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms . (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.)
They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry.

These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race .)
PitPro’s first tire-changing robot goes live in Canada Sean O'Kane
Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover.

On retailers like Amazon and Walmart, and marketplaces like eBay and Etsy , there are thousands of Apple Watch keychains, straps, pendants, lanyards, clips, and bag charm cases now available in nearly every style you can think of.

This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend , which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs , cassette tapes, home phones , and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback.

extraction.body: Is Meta’s just-announced Muse Charm a playful device that will make AI more approachable to everyday consumers, or will it be yet another flop in a long list of AI hardware gadgets that didn’t take off, like the Ai Pin, Rabbit, or Friend pendant? Reactions, so far, have been mixed. What the Charm is, however, is on-trend. Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post- Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags. It’s all part of a broader kitschy, retro-inspired shift in their approach to fashion and technology. Already, Gen Z has created a market for things that dangle, with everything from lip glosses to hand sanitizers to sunblocks to fragrances and more turned into bag charms , primarily targeted at women. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kristina Rodulfo (@kristinarodulfo) Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case , had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms . (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.) Then there was the Labubu craze , which saw sales of the so-ugly-it’s-cute fuzzy monster bag charm explode, growing Pop Mart’s (the Chinese retailer behind the product) revenue to $1.8 billion in 2024 , a 7x jump from 2019. While demand for the Labubu itself has since faded, the concept of the decorative bag charm has not. One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030 . Today, bag charms can be characters, bedazzled beauty products, or other whimsical designs or objects, like Coach’s coveted cherry charms , a Gen Z favorite . They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry. Similarly, Meta’s Muse is a customizable character; you design your own avatar, which makes the AI agent a reflection of you, too. And, as many have pointed out, Muse Charm’s form factor recalls a Tamagotchi, the pocket-sized digital virtual pet that became a major toy fad in the late 90s and again in the mid-2000s. However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference. It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch. As you might expect, these keychain watches are often being adopted by younger women as a fashion accessory first, rather than a piece of technology. I’m obsessed 💕 #applewatch #teacher #teachersoftiktok #girly #cute This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend , which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs , cassette tapes, home phones , and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback. This vibe shift in tech comes as young people describe the addictive, algorithm-driven feeds and “soulness” nature of technology as making them feel more disconnected, which has also fed into this trend of wanting tech they can touch and feel. (One startup, Clicks, is even bringing back the physical phone keyboard in a BlackBerry-inspired device , for instance.) For Gen Z, these physical objects help them feel more connected with the technology they’re using and offer a sense of control over a world where technology has become so deeply integrated into our lives that it no longer feels like a choice to use it. Young women , again, have been at the forefront of this trend, with some even crafting their own portable, mini computers, “cyberdecks, ” which they fit inside clamshell purses or custom cases, and bedazzle with jewels, flowers, stickers, pearls, and other items to make them feel more personal. That brings us back to the Muse Charm. While it’s clearly designed with the tech-as-fashion-accessory trend in mind, that doesn’t mean it will be a hit. Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover. To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations. In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement. It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses. These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race .) Meta’s end game, after all, is highly-targeted, highly-personalized ads. Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case , had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms . (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.)

Then there was the Labubu craze , which saw sales of the so-ugly-it’s-cute fuzzy monster bag charm explode, growing Pop Mart’s (the Chinese retailer behind the product) revenue to $1.8 billion in 2024 , a 7x jump from 2019. While demand for the Labubu itself has since faded, the concept of the decorative bag charm has not. One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030 .

Today, bag charms can be characters, bedazzled beauty products, or other whimsical designs or objects, like Coach’s coveted cherry charms , a Gen Z favorite . They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry.
Similarly, Meta’s Muse is a customizable character; you design your own avatar, which makes the AI agent a reflection of you, too.
And, as many have pointed out, Muse Charm’s form factor recalls a Tamagotchi, the pocket-sized digital virtual pet that became a major toy fad in the late 90s and again in the mid-2000s.

However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference. It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch. Often meant as a way to repurpose an older device , the concept of the Apple Watch keychain or charm has been growing in popularity, fueled by TikTok videos showing different ways to use the watch when not on your wrist.

On retailers like Amazon and Walmart, and marketplaces like eBay and Etsy , there are thousands of Apple Watch keychains, straps, pendants, lanyards, clips, and bag charm cases now available in nearly every style you can think of. As you might expect, these keychain watches are often being adopted by younger women as a fashion accessory first, rather than a piece of technology.

This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend , which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs , cassette tapes, home phones , and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback.

This vibe shift in tech comes as young people describe the addictive, algorithm-driven feeds and “soulness” nature of technology as making them feel more disconnected, which has also fed into this trend of wanting tech they can touch and feel. (One startup, Clicks, is even bringing back the physical phone keyboard in a BlackBerry-inspired device , for instance.)

For Gen Z, these physical objects help them feel more connected with the technology they’re using and offer a sense of control over a world where technology has become so deeply integrated into our lives that it no longer feels like a choice to use it.

Young women , again, have been at the forefront of this trend, with some even crafting their own portable, mini computers, “cyberdecks, ” which they fit inside clamshell purses or custom cases, and bedazzle with jewels, flowers, stickers, pearls, and other items to make them feel more personal.
That brings us back to the Muse Charm. While it’s clearly designed with the tech-as-fashion-accessory trend in mind, that doesn’t mean it will be a hit.
Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover.

To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations. In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement. It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses.

These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race .)

Meta’s end game, after all, is highly-targeted, highly-personalized ads. If that’s the privacy tradeoff in gaining access to free AI — Meta said it will monetize Muse by taking a small fee from transactions — consumers could be willing to take the risk.

Reactions, so far, have been mixed. What the Charm is, however, is on-trend. Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post- Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags. It’s all part of a broader kitschy, retro-inspired shift in their approach to fashion and technology. Already, Gen Z has created a market for things that dangle, with everything from lip glosses to hand sanitizers to sunblocks to fragrances and more turned into bag charms , primarily targeted at women. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kristina Rodulfo (@kristinarodulfo) Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case , had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms . (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.) Then there was the Labubu craze , which saw sales of the so-ugly-it’s-cute fuzzy monster bag charm explode, growing Pop Mart’s (the Chinese retailer behind the product) revenue to $1.8 billion in 2024 , a 7x jump from 2019. While demand for the Labubu itself has since faded, the concept of the decorative bag charm has not. One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030 . Today, bag charms can be characters, bedazzled beauty products, or other whimsical designs or objects, like Coach’s coveted cherry charms , a Gen Z favorite . They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry. Similarly, Meta’s Muse is a customizable character; you design your own avatar, which makes the AI agent a reflection of you, too. And, as many have pointed out, Muse Charm’s form factor recalls a Tamagotchi, the pocket-sized digital virtual pet that became a major toy fad in the late 90s and again in the mid-2000s. However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference. It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch. As you might expect, these keychain watches are often being adopted by younger women as a fashion accessory first, rather than a piece of technology. I’m obsessed 💕 #applewatch #teacher #teachersoftiktok #girly #cute This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend , which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs , cassette tapes, home phones , and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback. This vibe shift in tech comes as young people describe the addictive, algorithm-driven feeds and “soulness” nature of technology as making them feel more disconnected, which has also fed into this trend of wanting tech they can touch and feel. (One startup, Clicks, is even bringing back the physical phone keyboard in a BlackBerry-inspired device , for instance.) For Gen Z, these physical objects help them feel more connected with the technology they’re using and offer a sense of control over a world where technology has become so deeply integrated into our lives that it no longer feels like a choice to use it. Young women , again, have been at the forefront of this trend, with some even crafting their own portable, mini computers, “cyberdecks, ” which they fit inside clamshell purses or custom cases, and bedazzle with jewels, flowers, stickers, pearls, and other items to make them feel more personal. That brings us back to the Muse Charm. While it’s clearly designed with the tech-as-fashion-accessory trend in mind, that doesn’t mean it will be a hit. Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover. To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations. In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement. It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses. These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race .) Meta’s end game, after all, is highly-targeted, highly-personalized ads. If that’s the privacy tradeoff in gaining access to free AI — Meta said it will monetize Muse by taking a small fee from transactions — consumers could be willing to take the risk. extraction.body: ⁠Attorneys for Arnold Schwarzenegger have asked a Los Angeles judge for amped-up security at a forthcoming court date in which the former actor and politician is expected to testify. The trial is set to determine the payout for Cheryl Augustine, who was involved in a 2022 four-vehicle traffic accident in which she claims Schwarzenegger's reckless driving caused her significant, life-altering injuries. Dordick posted a mock-movie advertisement that included a description and photo of the 2022 incident as well as the time, date and location of the upcoming court date. The post also featured Dordick dressed like the Terminator, with the signature shades and leather jacket. Now attorneys for the former action hero, 79, are requesting that court officials and law enforcement set up security protocols; disallow photography, video or audio recording; and tighten up who's allowed in the courtroom. The legal filing, obtained by The Times, argues that Dordick's post "tells any one of Instagram’s three billion active users the date, time, street address, department number, and expected duration of Arnold Schwarzenegger’s attendance at trial in a public courthouse." The filing acknowledges that the information is already publicly available but argues that the post "goes further, through a ubiquitous medium that does not call for a citizen to navigate the Los Angeles County Superior Court’s website." "Indeed, the post identifies Governor Schwarzenegger as the first witness," the filing reads. "Whatever else may be said about the post, it is an advertisement for the appearance of one of the most recognizable people in the world at a fixed place and time, published five weeks in advance, by a person who has no responsibility for what happens when the audience shows up." In Augustine's Beverly Hills Superior Court lawsuit, she claims that Schwarzenegger was negligent when his SUV sped through a left turn at the intersection of Sunset Boulevard and Allenford Avenue, and struck her Toyota Prius, along with a Porsche and another Toyota. At the time, Los Angeles police said that paramedics transported a woman who suffered a head abrasion to the hospital. Schwarzenegger has admitted he was negligent but disputes the amount of damages Augustine is requesting. In 2023, the former governor and his GMC Yukon were the subject of another accident-turned-lawsuit. Joanne Flickinger sued Schwarzenegger for negligent driving which she claimed led to the biking accident that landed her with hefty medical bills. The suit, reviewed by The Times, states that on Feb. 5, 2023, Schwarzenegger was driving “with excessive speed and failed to keep a proper lookout” on San Vicente Boulevard when his vehicle struck Flickinger, “causing severe injuries.” The suit further alleges that Flickinger’s injuries are “permanent.”

"Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," Oracle said in a statement to CNBC. "We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward." That includes local opposition to data centers ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and concerns from environmental groups. The site has also faced delays with the buildout of a natural gas pipeline intended to fuel the facility. Shares of Bloom Energy, which is slated to power the more than 2.4-gigawatt facility with its fuel cells, fell 3% on the news. In a post to X, the company said it remains "committed" to the contract and following the "planned timeline." Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk told analysts on the company's earnings call on Sept. 10 that Project Jupiter would not affect its previously stated fiscal 2027 revenue or earnings guidance. Concerns have also mounted over Oracle's $18 billion in debt tied to the data center, which is already trading at stressed levels, according to the Financial Times. — CNBC's Seema Mody and Leslie Picker contributed reporting. passages: Oracle has sent a force majeure notice to the developer of Project Jupiter, a Stargate data center campus in New Mexico, Bloomberg first reported Thursday.
Force majeure clauses, common in energy and commodities contracts, excuse a party from contractual obligations when events outside its control get in the way.
Oracle is not seeking to exit as the campus’s main tenant, according to Bloomberg’s sources.
Instead, the notice would allow the company to delay payments should the facility miss its 2028 target to come online.
Oracle maintains that it does not expect a delay.
“Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule,” Oracle said in a statement to CNBC .
“We are fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward.”
Project Jupiter is one of the flagship sites of Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative Oracle, OpenAI, and SoftBank announced with President Donald Trump early in his second term.
The campus has drawn opposition from residents and environmental groups and has become a political flashpoint ahead of the midterm elections.
The notice also comes as AI data center construction faces growing scrutiny nationally, and as developers take on steep costs to build capacity for customers like OpenAI.

extraction.body: Oracle shares dropped about 4% in premarket trading Thursday after Bloomberg News reported the software giant is invoking a "force majeure" clause to shield itself from potential cost overruns on a major data center project in New Mexico. The company sent the notice to a developer controlled by Blue Owl Capital, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. Blue Owl, a publicly traded asset manager, also saw its shares fall. Reuters said it could not independently verify the information. At issue is a facility dubbed Project Jupiter, which Oracle is slated to anchor as its main tenant. Rather than walking away from the project, Oracle is seeking to delay payments if the data center gets derailed and fails to come online in 2028 as planned, according to the report. Project Jupiter covers about 1,400 acres in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, and is one of the sites announced under Stargate, the AI infrastructure venture formed by OpenAI, Oracle, SoftBank and Abu Dhabi's MGX. The campus is designed around four data center buildings, an on-site microgrid, battery storage and a desalination plant. The $165 billion figure that has attached itself to the project is a ceiling rather than committed capital. Doña Ana County approved up to that amount in industrial revenue bonds over a 30-year financing term, and the developers' plan calls for an initial $50 billion of investment within five years. Force majeure provisions are typically invoked to release parties from contractual obligations when circumstances beyond their control disrupt performance. The project has run into a series of obstacles. On Sept. 17, the New Mexico Supreme Court allowed permitting proceedings to resume after temporarily pausing an air-quality case and the use of an emergency construction well, though the unanimous orders did not decide whether regulators should grant the permits. The air-quality application covers the campus's proposed on-site power system. A gas pipeline meant to feed that system has twice been denied approval for a segment crossing state land and may not enter service until early 2027, while local opposition and environmental concerns have sharpened ahead of the midterm elections. Both companies pushed back on the report. "Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," Oracle said in a statement, adding that it is "fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward." Blue Owl said the notice "does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project." Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk told analysts on the company's Sept. 10 earnings call that the project would not affect its previously stated fiscal 2027 revenue or earnings guidance. The financial stakes reach beyond the two companies. Roughly $18 billion of debt tied to the Oracle-leased campus has been quoted at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar in private quotes from syndicate banks, and is already trading at stressed levels, the Financial Times reported. The stock decline reflects investor unease over potential friction in Oracle's aggressive data center expansion, a cornerstone of its push to capture growing demand for cloud infrastructure and AI workloads. Bloomberg was first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter. The company is looking to delay payment on the campus, dubbed Project Jupiter, if it fails to come online as expected in 2028, according to the report. That includes local opposition to data centers ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and concerns from environmental groups. The site has also faced delays with the buildout of a natural gas pipeline intended to fuel the facility. Shares of Bloom Energy, which is slated to power the more than 2.4-gigawatt facility with its fuel cells, fell 3% on the news. In a post to X, the company said it remains "committed" to the contract and following the "planned timeline." Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk told analysts on the company's earnings call on Sept. 10 that Project Jupiter would not affect its previously stated fiscal 2027 revenue or earnings guidance. Concerns have also mounted over Oracle's $18 billion in debt tied to the data center, which is already trading at stressed levels, according to the Financial Times. — CNBC's Seema Mody and Leslie Picker contributed reporting. The company sent the notice to a developer controlled by Blue Owl Capital, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. Blue Owl, a publicly traded asset manager, also saw its shares fall. Reuters said it could not independently verify the information. At issue is a facility dubbed Project Jupiter, which Oracle is slated to anchor as its main tenant. Rather than walking away from the project, Oracle is seeking to delay payments if the data center gets derailed and fails to come online in 2028 as planned, according to the report. Project Jupiter covers about 1,400 acres in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, and is one of the sites announced under Stargate, the AI infrastructure venture formed by OpenAI, Oracle, SoftBank and Abu Dhabi's MGX. The campus is designed around four data center buildings, an on-site microgrid, battery storage and a desalination plant. The $165 billion figure that has attached itself to the project is a ceiling rather than committed capital. Doña Ana County approved up to that amount in industrial revenue bonds over a 30-year financing term, and the developers' plan calls for an initial $50 billion of investment within five years. Force majeure provisions are typically invoked to release parties from contractual obligations when circumstances beyond their control disrupt performance. The project has run into a series of obstacles. On Sept. 17, the New Mexico Supreme Court allowed permitting proceedings to resume after temporarily pausing an air-quality case and the use of an emergency construction well, though the unanimous orders did not decide whether regulators should grant the permits. The air-quality application covers the campus's proposed on-site power system. A gas pipeline meant to feed that system has twice been denied approval for a segment crossing state land and may not enter service until early 2027, while local opposition and environmental concerns have sharpened ahead of the midterm elections. Both companies pushed back on the report. "Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule," Oracle said in a statement, adding that it is "fully committed to New Mexico and confident in our path forward." Blue Owl said the notice "does not change the financial commitments to this multi-year project." sources.title: Google's first Suncatcher orbital data center test launches October 1
passages: Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers .
Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .
With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions.
The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”
Google’s experimental orbital data center will have four TPUs and only run for 15 minutes at a time.
Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches.
This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.
Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers.
Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat.
AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison.
Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes.
Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator.
Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports.
That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer.
Google did not build the satellite from scratch.
The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts.
So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously.
After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.
Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges.
For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions.
Radiation can damage chips or simply interfere with calculations by flipping bits.
But vibration and high g-forces during launch also pose problems.
Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there.

The spacecraft was built in partnership with satellite imagery firm Planet Labs.
The mission will assess how Google’s TPUs withstand launch forces, radiation, and thermal extremes.
Google said its Trillium TPUs held up well in ground tests, surviving radiation doses greater than what a five-year space mission would deliver.
In space, there’s no airflow; heat must be diffused via radiators.
Google’s design combines heat pipes and radiators, but the system can only run in roughly 15-minute bursts before the TPUs must shut down to let radiators catch up.

facts.text: Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers .
Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .
With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions.
The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”
Google’s experimental orbital data center will have four TPUs and only run for 15 minutes at a time.
Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches.
This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.
Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers.
Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat.
AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison.
Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes.
Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator.
Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports.
That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer.
Google did not build the satellite from scratch.
The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts.
So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously.
After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.
Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges.
For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions.
Radiation can damage chips or simply interfere with calculations by flipping bits.
But vibration and high g-forces during launch also pose problems.
Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there.

Future designs envision clusters of satellites carrying dozens of TPUs each, communicating via high-bandwidth lasers.
Google plans to launch two satellites in 2027 to test those laser links.
The refrigerator-sized satellite, named MVP, will carry four of Google’s custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.
The spacecraft was built in partnership with satellite imagery firm Planet Labs.
The mission will assess how Google’s TPUs withstand launch forces, radiation, and thermal extremes.
Google said its Trillium TPUs held up well in ground tests, surviving radiation doses greater than what a five-year space mission would deliver.
In space, there’s no airflow; heat must be diffused via radiators.
Google’s design combines heat pipes and radiators, but the system can only run in roughly 15-minute bursts before the TPUs must shut down to let radiators catch up.

story.title: Google's first Suncatcher orbital data center test launches October 1

facts.text: Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers .
Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .
With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions.
The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”
Google’s experimental orbital data center will have four TPUs and only run for 15 minutes at a time.
Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches.
This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.
Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers.
Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat.
AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison.
Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes.
Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator.
Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports.
That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer.
Google did not build the satellite from scratch.
The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts.
So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously.
After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.
Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges.
For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions.
Radiation can damage chips or simply interfere with calculations by flipping bits.
But vibration and high g-forces during launch also pose problems.
Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there.
Google under Alphabet Inc. (GOOG) is preparing to launch its first experimental satellite as part of Project Suncatcher, an ambitious effort to develop AI data centers in orbit.
The spacecraft was built by Planet Labs, allowing Google to accelerate its testing rather than develop a satellite from scratch.
Google plans additional launches in 2027 but expects Suncatcher will remain years away from becoming a commercial product.

sources.title: Microsoft thinks its new Copilot ‘super app’ will be as influential as Office
passages: Microsoft is even comparing its new Copilot to how influential Office was on productivity.
“Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era,” says Spataro.
With this new Copilot app it feels like Microsoft has finally settled on a formula for its AI assistant.
The real difference against some other AI agents is that Microsoft has made Autopilot enterprise grade, appealing to businesses that rely on its Office and identity management suites.

It’s the default landing experience for Copilot users, and Microsoft is also planning to include a Today feature inside it that works as a personalized dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more.
It’s fair to say that Copilot has failed in the consumer space compared to Claude or ChatGPT, but Microsoft’s core commercial customers are slowly showing interest.
“We’re building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task,” says Nadella in a post on X.
The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents.

Microsoft is using an auto model picker to match the model for each task, but IT admins will need to use Microsoft’s new FinOps for AI to manage AI spend and ensure any agentic usage doesn’t get out of control.

The company has redesigned Copilot plenty of times since its introduction as a chatbot inside Bing, and this latest three-tab design builds on the combination of its two separate consumer and commercial Copilot apps last month.
Code will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.
Microsoft has certainly fallen behind the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Meta, and it’ll be interesting to see if “the AI built for work” is enough to help it catch up.
The difference this time around is that how much a business pays for Copilot will depend on what their employees are doing.
The regular Copilot license, known as a user subscription license, will give you Copilot in Chat, and in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams.
That’s a long-overdue change, alongside some big AI leadership shapeups that helped finally appoint a single Copilot boss for the first time.

extraction.body: After teasing its new Copilot “super app” last month, Microsoft is officially unveiling it today. The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents. As part of the launch, Microsoft is also rebranding Scout, the AI personal assistant it unveiled at Build earlier this year, as Autopilot. This new Copilot app will have three tabs for Home, Code, and Autopilot, with Home combining Copilot Chat and Cowork together. It’s the default landing experience for Copilot users, and Microsoft is also planning to include a Today feature inside it that works as a personalized dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more. It will let anyone create an app, tracker, dashboard, or automation and share the results with colleagues as cloud-hosted internal apps. “Powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot, Code runs in a sandboxed environment and can be hosted securely within your tenant,” says Spataro. Autopilot is a new addition to the Copilot experience, and one that Spataro describes as a “digital teammate.” Previously called Scout and available initially as a desktop app, Autopilot is the cloud equivalent that enables a personal AI assistant to keep running while you’re asleep. Like many other AI agents, Autopilot has its own cloud computer instance that can be tasked to do things like watch Teams channels, run recurring work tasks, or handle follow-ups. The real difference against some other AI agents is that Microsoft has made Autopilot enterprise grade, appealing to businesses that rely on its Office and identity management suites. “Autopilot lives in your tenant with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace, and it’s built on Microsoft IQ so it understands how your organization actually works,” says Spataro. The difference this time around is that how much a business pays for Copilot will depend on what their employees are doing. Microsoft is using usage-based billing for the Cowork, Code, and Autopilot parts of this new Copilot app, so any long-running agentic capabilities or usage of models like Astra and Fable will be billed based on usage. The regular Copilot license, known as a user subscription license, will give you Copilot in Chat, and in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams. Microsoft is using an auto model picker to match the model for each task, but IT admins will need to use Microsoft’s new FinOps for AI to manage AI spend and ensure any agentic usage doesn’t get out of control. With this new Copilot app it feels like Microsoft has finally settled on a formula for its AI assistant. The company has redesigned Copilot plenty of times since its introduction as a chatbot inside Bing, and this latest three-tab design builds on the combination of its two separate consumer and commercial Copilot apps last month. That’s a long-overdue change, alongside some big AI leadership shapeups that helped finally appoint a single Copilot boss for the first time. The new Home and Code tabs will start rolling out to Microsoft’s Frontier program for early access AI features “in the coming weeks,” and Autopilot will go into private preview later this month. Code will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year. It’s fair to say that Copilot has failed in the consumer space compared to Claude or ChatGPT, but Microsoft’s core commercial customers are slowly showing interest. This new Copilot app isn’t really designed to compete with things like Muse, and Microsoft is now calling it “the AI built for work.” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also calls Copilot a new operating system. “We’re building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task,” says Nadella in a post on X. Microsoft is even comparing its new Copilot to how influential Office was on productivity. “Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era,” says Spataro. That might well be Microsoft’s goal, but there’s a lot more competition in this AI era than there ever was in the PC era. Microsoft has certainly fallen behind the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Meta, and it’ll be interesting to see if “the AI built for work” is enough to help it catch up. The new Home and Code tabs will start rolling out to Microsoft’s Frontier program for early access AI features “in the coming weeks,” and Autopilot will go into private preview later this month.
Code will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.
It’s fair to say that Copilot has failed in the consumer space compared to Claude or ChatGPT, but Microsoft’s core commercial customers are slowly showing interest.

This new Copilot app isn’t really designed to compete with things like Muse, and Microsoft is now calling it “the AI built for work.” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella also calls Copilot a new operating system.
“We’re building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task,” says Nadella in a post on X.
Microsoft is even comparing its new Copilot to how influential Office was on productivity.

sources.title: Microsoft unveils Copilot super app, targeting business users with AI agents - Fortune
passages: Microsoft is betting the super app will supercharge its Copilot brand by using AI directly connected to the business tools that already make it money.
As OpenAI and Anthropic push into enterprise offerings, Microsoft is racing to protect its turf and keep pace with customer expectations.
It’s also launching the app just as agentic capabilities break into the mainstream.
Meta Platforms has already seen early success with its new Muse app, which targets general consumers, letting them create a personal agent to handle food orders, bank statements, and other tasks.
The launch follows a push by Microsoft to merge what had become a sprawling collection of Copilot products that critics said left customers confused.
Both enterprise customers and individual users will have to pay extra based on usage of its most autonomous capabilities.
After the AI boom took off about four years ago, Microsoft poured resources into winning both the consumer and enterprise sides of AI.
Microsoft’s super app reveal also follows a stretch of growing pains for Copilot.
Copilot stumbled early, plagued by branding issues, limited capabilities, and Microsoft’s decision to launch several versions of the AI that confused customers.
Its consumer Copilot failed to reach mainstream success.
More recently, as Microsoft has refocused on enterprise and streamlined its operations, it’s found some traction.
In July, the company said its Microsoft 365 Copilot had surpassed 30 million paid seats, with net seats added doubling quarter over quarter.
Its shares have rebounded over the past six months on the strength of its cloud computing business, fueled by AI demand and Copilot growth.
“We do want this to become an all-in-one productivity suite,” Annie Pearl, corporate vice president of Copilot, told Fortune .

That includes being a platform “where you can ask questions, you could delegate complex multi-step work, you can build software for internal and external use cases, and you can automate tasks through your kind of digital worker or personal agent.”

For Chief Executive Satya Nadella, the new Copilot is a way to win subscriptions in a business that’s become increasingly important to the software maker, while also ensuring that Microsoft’s lucrative productivity offerings don’t get sidelined by a new generation of AI rivals.
The coding tool, which shares its underlying tech stack with Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, will reach Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers through the test program later this year.
Autopilot will undergo a more restricted phase of user testing, and broad rollout will hinge on how testers rate the new tools.
“Everything that you observe should be governable by policy,” Nadella told customers this week at a presentation at Microsoft’s Redmond, Wash. headquarters.
“That’s the classic thing we have done for decades when it comes to IT management, and now I need to do that with every agent out there.
Copilot relies mostly on models from Anthropic and OpenAI, though it also accesses xAI’s Grok models, Pearl said.
On Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government website in June, marking the latest such incident.
Microsoft said it has built several safety guards into its app.
Those include rules requiring its Autopilot agents to carry explicit permissions, full audit logs, and tracking.
When non-developers build apps using the Code tool, the software runs tasks in isolated local or cloud-hosted environments, with controls intended to protect customer data and systems.
Microsoft also plans to monetize the new features by charging extra for its best capabilities.
“The way we have conceptualized Copilot is to think of this not as just any one product or one form factor, but as a system that brings form and function together.”
That includes a function called “Today,” which Microsoft says will integrate emails, calendar, Teams, and tasks to organize and prioritize workloads.

The Autopilot feature lets users name their agent, assign it a role and a goal, then set it loose on tasks such as project updates, tracking work decisions and deadlines, reminding colleagues when commitments are due, gathering prep materials, and reaching out to partners.

extraction.body: After the AI boom took off about four years ago, Microsoft poured resources into winning both the consumer and enterprise sides of AI. With the unveiling of its Copilot AI “super app” Friday, the software giant has returned to basics, aiming its most capable technology at business customers. Microsoft is launching its super app as a central interface through which customers can chat with AI bots, tap AI tools to help accomplish tasks, write code, and access a new “Autopilot” feature that brings agentic capabilities — AI that can act on tasks on its own — to the company’s flagship AI app. The super app is a major redesign of Microsoft’s existing Copilot app, bringing together a variety of features and capabilities intended to create a Swiss Army knife for AI productivity. The launch follows a push by Microsoft to merge what had become a sprawling collection of Copilot products that critics said left customers confused. For Chief Executive Satya Nadella, the new Copilot is a way to win subscriptions in a business that’s become increasingly important to the software maker, while also ensuring that Microsoft’s lucrative productivity offerings don’t get sidelined by a new generation of AI rivals. The super app, first reported by Fortune in May , also plugs into Microsoft’s Office tools, letting users ask a bot to handle a task on an Excel spreadsheet or change a layout in a Word document. Though there is a free version of the super app, customers will need their Microsoft subscriptions or workplace licenses to unlock its full range of offerings. Both enterprise customers and individual users will have to pay extra based on usage of its most autonomous capabilities. “We do want this to become an all-in-one productivity suite,” Annie Pearl, corporate vice president of Copilot, told Fortune . That includes being a platform “where you can ask questions, you could delegate complex multi-step work, you can build software for internal and external use cases, and you can automate tasks through your kind of digital worker or personal agent.” The Autopilot feature lets users name their agent, assign it a role and a goal, then set it loose on tasks such as project updates, tracking work decisions and deadlines, reminding colleagues when commitments are due, gathering prep materials, and reaching out to partners. The coding feature targets non-software engineers who want to build apps, a dashboard, or other tools and platforms, Pearl said, though she added that it will grow more powerful over time. Most of the app’s new features are rolling out through an early-test program, and Microsoft has not set a timeline for general availability. The coding tool, which shares its underlying tech stack with Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, will reach Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers through the test program later this year. Autopilot will undergo a more restricted phase of user testing, and broad rollout will hinge on how testers rate the new tools. Microsoft is betting the super app will supercharge its Copilot brand by using AI directly connected to the business tools that already make it money. As OpenAI and Anthropic push into enterprise offerings, Microsoft is racing to protect its turf and keep pace with customer expectations. It’s also launching the app just as agentic capabilities break into the mainstream. OpenAI unveiled its own super app in July. Meta Platforms has already seen early success with its new Muse app, which targets general consumers, letting them create a personal agent to handle food orders, bank statements, and other tasks. Microsoft’s super app reveal also follows a stretch of growing pains for Copilot. Nadella has shaken up executive ranks to position the company competitively against the top AI labs and enterprise rivals, forging a unified Copilot team earlier this year that merged the consumer and enterprise sides under Jacob Andreou, the fast-rising executive now in charge of Copilot. Copilot stumbled early, plagued by branding issues, limited capabilities, and Microsoft’s decision to launch several versions of the AI that confused customers. Its consumer Copilot failed to reach mainstream success. More recently, as Microsoft has refocused on enterprise and streamlined its operations, it’s found some traction. In July, the company said its Microsoft 365 Copilot had surpassed 30 million paid seats, with net seats added doubling quarter over quarter. Its shares have rebounded over the past six months on the strength of its cloud computing business, fueled by AI demand and Copilot growth. Copilot relies mostly on models from Anthropic and OpenAI, though it also accesses xAI’s Grok models, Pearl said. Security has also been a top concern, especially as models from OpenAI and Anthropic have been used to hack into other companies in recent months, stoking worldwide unease about AI capabilities. On Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government website in June, marking the latest such incident. Microsoft said it has built several safety guards into its app. Those include rules requiring its Autopilot agents to carry explicit permissions, full audit logs, and tracking. Humans decide how much autonomy an agent receives, the company said. When non-developers build apps using the Code tool, the software runs tasks in isolated local or cloud-hosted environments, with controls intended to protect customer data and systems. “Everything that you observe should be governable by policy,” Nadella told customers this week at a presentation at Microsoft’s Redmond, Wash. headquarters. “That’s the classic thing we have done for decades when it comes to IT management, and now I need to do that with every agent out there. “The way we have conceptualized Copilot is to think of this not as just any one product or one form factor, but as a system that brings form and function together.” Microsoft also plans to monetize the new features by charging extra for its best capabilities. Seats paid for by enterprise customers or individual users cover “everyday AI” such as Chat, Office integration, and standard routing, while usage-based billing can apply to Code, Autopilot, and access to the newest, most capable AI models. Microsoft also plans future add-ons that would tie in even more of its ecosystem. That includes a function called “Today,” which Microsoft says will integrate emails, calendar, Teams, and tasks to organize and prioritize workloads. It will actively complete tasks, such as generating drafts, proposing schedule updates, and setting up follow-ups for quick user action, the company said.

coreStoryFacts.text: Microsoft is even comparing its new Copilot to how influential Office was on productivity.
“Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era,” says Spataro.
With this new Copilot app it feels like Microsoft has finally settled on a formula for its AI assistant.
The real difference against some other AI agents is that Microsoft has made Autopilot enterprise grade, appealing to businesses that rely on its Office and identity management suites.

It’s the default landing experience for Copilot users, and Microsoft is also planning to include a Today feature inside it that works as a personalized dashboard for important emails, meeting requests, Teams threads, and more.
It’s fair to say that Copilot has failed in the consumer space compared to Claude or ChatGPT, but Microsoft’s core commercial customers are slowly showing interest.
“We’re building Copilot as a new OS for work that spans every model, every form factor, and every task,” says Nadella in a post on X.
The redesigned Copilot app bundles three AI capabilities into a single interface of chat, coding, and agents.

Microsoft is using an auto model picker to match the model for each task, but IT admins will need to use Microsoft’s new FinOps for AI to manage AI spend and ensure any agentic usage doesn’t get out of control.

The company has redesigned Copilot plenty of times since its introduction as a chatbot inside Bing, and this latest three-tab design builds on the combination of its two separate consumer and commercial Copilot apps last month.
Code will also be in preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.
Microsoft has certainly fallen behind the likes of Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and now Meta, and it’ll be interesting to see if “the AI built for work” is enough to help it catch up.
The difference this time around is that how much a business pays for Copilot will depend on what their employees are doing.
The regular Copilot license, known as a user subscription license, will give you Copilot in Chat, and in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams.
That’s a long-overdue change, alongside some big AI leadership shapeups that helped finally appoint a single Copilot boss for the first time.
Microsoft is betting the super app will supercharge its Copilot brand by using AI directly connected to the business tools that already make it money.
As OpenAI and Anthropic push into enterprise offerings, Microsoft is racing to protect its turf and keep pace with customer expectations.
It’s also launching the app just as agentic capabilities break into the mainstream.
Meta Platforms has already seen early success with its new Muse app, which targets general consumers, letting them create a personal agent to handle food orders, bank statements, and other tasks.
The launch follows a push by Microsoft to merge what had become a sprawling collection of Copilot products that critics said left customers confused.
Both enterprise customers and individual users will have to pay extra based on usage of its most autonomous capabilities.
After the AI boom took off about four years ago, Microsoft poured resources into winning both the consumer and enterprise sides of AI.
Microsoft’s super app reveal also follows a stretch of growing pains for Copilot.
Copilot stumbled early, plagued by branding issues, limited capabilities, and Microsoft’s decision to launch several versions of the AI that confused customers.

The Autopilot feature lets users name their agent, assign it a role and a goal, then set it loose on tasks such as project updates, tracking work decisions and deadlines, reminding colleagues when commitments are due, gathering prep materials, and reaching out to partners.
The coding feature targets non-software engineers who want to build apps, a dashboard, or other tools and platforms, Pearl said, though she added that it will grow more powerful over time.

Most of the app’s new features are rolling out through an early-test program, and Microsoft has not set a timeline for general availability. The coding tool, which shares its underlying tech stack with Microsoft’s GitHub Copilot, will reach Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers through the test program later this year. Autopilot will undergo a more restricted phase of user testing, and broad rollout will hinge on how testers rate the new tools.

Microsoft is betting the super app will supercharge its Copilot brand by using AI directly connected to the business tools that already make it money. As OpenAI and Anthropic push into enterprise offerings, Microsoft is racing to protect its turf and keep pace with customer expectations. It’s also launching the app just as agentic capabilities break into the mainstream. OpenAI unveiled its own super app in July. Meta Platforms has already seen early success with its new Muse app, which targets general consumers, letting them create a personal agent to handle food orders, bank statements, and other tasks.

Microsoft’s super app reveal also follows a stretch of growing pains for Copilot. Nadella has shaken up executive ranks to position the company competitively against the top AI labs and enterprise rivals, forging a unified Copilot team earlier this year that merged the consumer and enterprise sides under Jacob Andreou, the fast-rising executive now in charge of Copilot.

Copilot stumbled early, plagued by branding issues, limited capabilities, and Microsoft’s decision to launch several versions of the AI that confused customers. Its consumer Copilot failed to reach mainstream success. More recently, as Microsoft has refocused on enterprise and streamlined its operations, it’s found some traction. In July, the company said its Microsoft 365 Copilot had surpassed 30 million paid seats, with net seats added doubling quarter over quarter. Its shares have rebounded over the past six months on the strength of its cloud computing business, fueled by AI demand and Copilot growth.

Copilot relies mostly on models from Anthropic and OpenAI, though it also accesses xAI’s Grok models, Pearl said. Security has also been a top concern, especially as models from OpenAI and Anthropic have been used to hack into other companies in recent months, stoking worldwide unease about AI capabilities. On Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government website in June, marking the latest such incident.

Microsoft said it has built several safety guards into its app. Those include rules requiring its Autopilot agents to carry explicit permissions, full audit logs, and tracking. Humans decide how much autonomy an agent receives, the company said. When non-developers build apps using the Code tool, the software runs tasks in isolated local or cloud-hosted environments, with controls intended to protect customer data and systems.

“Everything that you observe should be governable by policy,” Nadella told customers this week at a presentation at Microsoft’s Redmond, Wash. headquarters. “That’s the classic thing we have done for decades when it comes to IT management, and now I need to do that with every agent out there.
“The way we have conceptualized Copilot is to think of this not as just any one product or one form factor, but as a system that brings form and function together.”

Microsoft also plans to monetize the new features by charging extra for its best capabilities. Seats paid for by enterprise customers or individual users cover “everyday AI” such as Chat, Office integration, and standard routing, while usage-based billing can apply to Code, Autopilot, and access to the newest, most capable AI models.

Microsoft also plans future add-ons that would tie in even more of its ecosystem. That includes a function called “Today,” which Microsoft says will integrate emails, calendar, Teams, and tasks to organize and prioritize workloads. It will actively complete tasks, such as generating drafts, proposing schedule updates, and setting up follow-ups for quick user action, the company said.
